w: Renamed four times before anyone settled on 'the Old Vic'. Manager Lilian Baylis made it a Shakespeare house from 1914, it took a bombing in the Blitz and kept going, and its own repertory company quietly became the National Theatre before that outfit grew up and moved to the South Bank in 1976.
s: Renamed four times before 'Old Vic' finally stuck
_facts: Established 1818 as the Royal Coburg Theatre; renamed Royal Victoria Theatre in 1833, then Royal Victoria Palace after an 1871 rebuild, then Royal Victoria Hall under Emma Cons from 1880
Lilian Baylis took over management in 1898 and began staging Shakespeare there from 1914
Damaged by air raids in 1940; became a Grade II* listed building after reopening

Its resident repertory company formed the core of the National Theatre of Great Britain on its 1963 founding under Laurence Olivier, until the National Theatre opened its own South Bank building in 1976

w: Built in 1711 for Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough - Queen Anne's fiercest confidante. It stayed a Marlborough town house for a century, then a royal one: two widowed queens, Alexandra and Mary, each retreated here in old age. Since 1965 it has quietly run the Commonwealth instead.
s: A duchess's mansion, later two widowed queens' retreat
_facts: Grade I listed mansion on The Mall in St James's, built in 1711 for Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough, confidante of Queen Anne
London residence of the Dukes of Marlborough for over a century before becoming a royal residence
Queen Alexandra and later Queen Mary each lived there as widows in old age
Leased by Queen Elizabeth II to the Commonwealth Secretariat from 1965, which still occupies it

w: Buffalo Bill's Wild West show pitched camp here in the 1880s, with Queen Victoria among the spectators - the start of a site that grew into an Art Moderne exhibition hall in the 1930s. Developers got a Certificate of Immunity from Listing before English Heritage could step in; the whole thing came down in 2017.
s: Vanished Art Deco hall where Buffalo Bill met the Queen
_facts: Site of exhibition and entertainment grounds opened in 1887, founded by Leeds entrepreneur John R. Whitley; first attraction was Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West show, seen by Queen Victoria
Art Moderne exhibition hall built 1935-37 by American architect C. Howard Crane
Developers were granted a Certificate of Immunity from Listing by English Heritage in 2008, blocking heritage protection
Demolition completed in 2017 as part of a redevelopment scheme

w: One of Europe's largest mosque complexes sits in unassuming Morden, paid for entirely by Ahmadi Muslim donations - built partly underground just to fit 13,000 worshippers in. Its Friday sermons go out live across a private global satellite network, and most weeks it's out feeding London's homeless too.
s: Europe's biggest mosque, built purely on donations
_facts: Ahmadiyya Muslim Community mosque complex in Morden, completed 2003 at a cost of GBP 15 million, funded entirely by donations from Ahmadi Muslims
One of the largest mosque complexes in Europe, accommodating up to 13,000 worshippers, extending below ground to maximise capacity
Hosts weekly Friday sermons by the Ahmadiyya Community's global head, relayed live via the MTA International satellite network
Known locally for homeless feeding and community cohesion work; featured in the 2015 Channel 5 documentary Britain's Biggest Mosque
